Chapter 3 — When Beliefs About Illness Collide.
Picture this: inside the hospital, it was impossible to miss just how differently the family and the medical team saw things. Every conversation, every decision—each side brought their own ideas about what it really means to be sick.
For the family, illness wasn’t just about the body. They believed the soul could wander, and that spirits might actually cause harm. For them, true healing needed more than just pills or injections—it needed rituals, traditions, and care for the spirit too. When their daughter’s seizures started, they saw it as a sign her soul had been taken. This wasn’t just a medical emergency to them—it was a crisis that needed a shaman, ceremonies, and offerings to restore balance and bring her back to health.
The doctors, on the other hand, saw things much more clinically. Seizures meant epilepsy—a condition they could manage with the right medication. They prescribed drugs, kept a close eye on her progress, and tweaked the treatment plan as needed. But to them, the family’s rituals seemed beside the point, or even risky, especially if they got in the way of medical care.
As days turned into weeks, this gap between the two approaches kept growing. The family struggled to stick to the medication schedule, sometimes missing doses or stopping treatment entirely. They worried about side effects—not just on their daughter’s body, but on her spirit as well. Was the medication making things worse? The doctors, meanwhile, grew frustrated. Why wasn’t the family following instructions? Why did it seem like they were rejecting the very help that could save their child?
Most people don’t realize just how much these misunderstandings can affect care. The doctors, focused on the science, missed the fear and confusion behind the family’s choices. The family, overwhelmed by the routines and rules of the hospital, didn’t know how to ask questions or voice their worries. Both sides felt misunderstood—and the one who suffered most was the child.
There were moments when things could’ve gone differently. What if someone had simply taken the time to listen? What if they’d asked about the family’s beliefs, or explained the treatment in a way that actually made sense to them? Maybe the outcome would have been very different. But in the rush of the hospital, with all its schedules and protocols, these chances often slipped by.
And you know what? This family’s story isn’t rare. All across the country, patients from all sorts of backgrounds run into the very same challenges. When beliefs about illness collide, the result is usually confusion, mistrust, and poor outcomes.
The truth is, great care takes more than just medical know-how. It takes real cultural understanding, humility, and a willingness to meet people where they are. That’s the lesson at the heart of this story—and it’s one we can’t afford to ignore.
